title: Breath, the life of all, and the third self, made of mind
theme: A verse praises breath as the life of every creature; then a third self, made of mind, appears inside the self of breath, and its limbs are the Vedas.

words.context: Śaṅkara: the breath that is air, having the power of breathing
Śaṅkara: Agni and the others; or, within the person, the senses

words.role: relative: ‘whatever humans and animals there are’

words.context: Śaṅkara: of the former, the self of food

words.meaning: from the one made of breath

words.context: Śaṅkara: mind is the inner organ of resolve and doubt
Śaṅkara and Rāmānanda: the mental activity that has the Yajus as its content
Śaṅkara: the Brāhmaṇa; Rāmānanda: injunction and prohibition; Kūranārāyaṇa: the teaching ‘that you are’ and the rules of ritual
the mantras seen by Atharvan and Aṅgiras

sandhi.type: final m; āḥ before a vowel
sandhi.rule: prāṇam → prāṇaṃ before d (P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः)); devāḥ before a loses its visarga and the hiatus stays (P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).
The visarga becomes ś before c.
P. 6.1.114 (हशि च): visarga → u, a + u → o.
m stays m before a vowel (no anusvāra).

sandhi.type: e before a vowel; visarga as r
sandhi.rule: te + ā: e becomes ay (P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः)) and the y drops (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)), leaving ta āyuḥ; the visarga after u becomes r before the voiced y.
tasya + e → ai; eṣaḥ before e and śārīraḥ before ā lose the visarga and keep the hiatus (P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).
yajuḥ (stem yajus): before a vowel the final s appears as r.
k → g before the voiced d: P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
Visarga lost before a vowel other than a, hiatus kept: P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य).

samasa.meaning: the life of all. Śaṅkara analyses it «सर्वेषामायुः सर्वायुः, सर्वायुरेव सर्वायुषम्».
made of mind, abounding in mind; Kūranārāyaṇa: «अत्र प्राचुर्यार्थो मयट्».

samasa.type: dvandva, used of the mantras they saw
samasa.vigraha: अथर्वा च अङ्गिराः च अथर्वाङ्गिरसौ, तैः दृष्टाः मन्त्राः अथर्वाङ्गिरसः
samasa.meaning: the mantras of Atharvan and Aṅgiras, i.e. of the Atharvaveda. Rāmānanda: «अथर्वा नाम कश्चिदृषिः, अङ्गिराश्च ताभ्यां दृष्टा मन्त्रा अथर्वाङ्गिरसः».

samasa.vigraha: पुरुषस्य विधा इव विधा यस्य सः पुरुषविधः

morphology.note: pra + an, ‘to breathe’; the n of the preverb’s ending conditions the cerebral ṇ. With anu, ‘breathe after, live by following’.
Taddhita from śarīra with vṛddhi of the first vowel: ‘belonging to, being in, the body’. Śaṅkara: «शरीरे अन्नमये भवः शारीरः».
Neuter s-stem āyus, ‘life, length of life’; nominative and accusative alike.
Nominative of the feminine c-stem ṛc, ‘verse’; final c becomes k in pause.
Nominative of the neuter n-stem sāman, ‘chant’; the n drops at the end of the word.
eṣaḥ written in its pre-consonantal form before pūrṇaḥ, as in 2.2 (the sandhi checker does not yet join eṣaḥ after the fusion tena + eṣaḥ).

translation.literal: Following breath the gods breathe, [and] the humans and animals, whichever [there are]. For breath [is] the life of beings; therefore it is called the life of all. They reach the whole lifespan who meditate on breath as Brahman. For breath [is] the life of beings; therefore it is called the life of all. Of that [one], this indeed [is] the embodied self — [of that] which [is] the former. From that, indeed, from this [self] made of breath, [there is] another, inner self, made of mind. By it this [one] is filled. That, indeed, this [one] is of a person’s shape. Following that one’s person-form, this one is of a person’s shape. Of it the Yajus indeed [is] the head; the Ṛc the right wing; the Sāman the left wing; instruction the trunk; the Atharvāṅgirasa the tail, the support. On that too there is this verse.
translation.readable: The gods breathe by breath, and so do humans and animals. Breath is the life of every being, so it is called the life of all. Those who revere breath as Brahman live out their full span. This self of breath is the embodied self of the one before it. Within the self of breath there is another self, made of mind, which fills it. It too has a person’s shape, following the shape of the self of breath: the Yajus is its head, the Ṛc its right side, the Sāman its left, instruction its body, the hymns of Atharvan and Aṅgiras its tail and support. There is a verse on this too.

syntax: As in 2.2: a verse (lines 1–8), then the fixed prose pattern. The verse has a main clause (prāṇaṃ devā anu prāṇanti) whose subject is extended by a relative (manuṣyāḥ paśavaś ca ye), reason and result clauses with hi and tasmāt, and a relative-correlative sentence (sarvam eva ta āyur yanti ye prāṇaṃ brahmopāsate). Lines 9–10 are a short nominal sentence with a relative clause (tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā yaḥ pūrvasya) whose reference is disputed. The prose then gives the self of mind and its five limbs, each a nominal sentence.

ambiguities.topic: tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā yaḥ pūrvasya
ambiguities.note: Two quite different readings. Śaṅkara: ‘of that former one (the self of food), this one (the self of breath) is the embodied self’ — «तस्य पूर्वस्य अन्नमयस्य एष एव शरीरे अन्नमये भवः शारीरः आत्मा»; each inner self is the self of the outer one. Kūranārāyaṇa: the self of the former, the supreme Self named in 2.1 (‘from that Self’), is also the embodied self of the self of breath — «स एव प्राणमयस्यापि शारीरः आत्मा». Gopālānanda takes śārīra as ‘the Self whose body all this is’ («यस्य इदं सर्वं शरीरं स शारीर आत्मा»), and Rāmānanda likewise moves the sense of ‘inner self’ beyond the self of breath. The words allow both.
Śaṅkara gives two senses: the gods such as Agni, or, in this inward context, the senses («अध्यात्माधिकारात् देवाः इन्द्रियाणि प्राणमनु प्राणन्ति»). Rāmānanda: the gods Indra, Brahmā and the rest.

ambiguities.topic: The Vedas as limbs of the self of mind
ambiguities.note: All the commentators take yajus, ṛc and sāman here not as words on a page but as the mind’s activity that has them as content (Rāmānanda: «यजुर्वेदार्थविषयकज्ञानोत्पादकमनोव्यापार एव»). They differ on ādeśa: the Brāhmaṇa portion of the Veda (Śaṅkara: «आदेशः अत्र ब्राह्मणम्»), injunction and prohibition (Rāmānanda: «आदेशो विधिनिषेधरूपः»), or the teaching and its rules (Kūranārāyaṇa).

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Lines 1–8 are the śloka announced at the end of 2.2, in short lines of about eight syllables; the rest is prose. Some lines as written differ from eight (line 5, with ta āyur, has 7); the edition does not regularise them.

beginner: This passage praises breath. The gods, people and animals all live by breathing; breath is the life of every creature, so it is called the life of all. Those who honour breath as the deepest reality, the text says, live out their full span. Then the text takes another step inward. Inside the self made of breath is a self made of mind, which fills it as breath fills the body. It too has a person’s shape, but its parts are surprising: its head, arms, body and tail are the different parts of the Veda — the sacrificial formulas, the verses, the chants, the instructions and the hymns of the Atharvaveda. The mind, on this picture, is shaped by what it learns and recites.
analogy: A singer who knows a song by heart can sing it silently; Śaṅkara argues that the Vedic mantras are the mind’s own activity, which is why they can be repeated silently in the mind.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: A verse says that gods, humans and animals live by breath; that breath is the life of beings and is called the life of all; and that those who meditate on breath as Brahman reach their full span. It says that this is the embodied self of the former. Prose names a third self, made of mind, inside the self of breath, and makes the Yajus, Ṛc, Sāman, instruction and the Atharvāṅgirasa its head, wings, trunk and tail.

commentary.q: What does it mean that breath is the ‘life of all’?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: beings are not selves only through the body; they have a self of breath common to all, pervading the whole body, and through it a self of mind and the rest, and finally the one Self beyond the five sheaths — «स हि परमार्थत आत्मा सर्वेषामित्येतदप्यर्थादुक्तं भवति». The fruit of meditating on breath as Brahman is the full lifespan, not dying before one’s time («नापमृत्युना म्रियन्ते प्राक्प्राप्तादायुष इत्यर्थः»).

commentary.q: Why are the Vedas the limbs of the mind?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: yajus is the head because the offering is made with Yajus formulas. But the deeper point is that the mantras, as known and recited, are activities of the mind: so the mind can repeat them silently («मानसो जप उपपद्यते»), and the Vedas can be eternal, being the consciousness of the Self conditioned by the mind’s activity. ādeśa is the Brāhmaṇa, which ‘enjoins what is to be enjoined’; the Atharvāṅgirasa is the tail because its rites of peace and prosperity give stability.

commentary.q: How do the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators read the passage?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Kūranārāyaṇa reads ‘the embodied self of the former’ as the supreme Self, already named in 2.1, which is also the self of the self of breath; the sheaths are its body. Rāmānanda takes the limbs as the mind’s activities that produce knowledge of each Veda, and reminds the reader that the five sheaths are imagined only to point to the supreme Self, as one shows the star Arundhatī by way of a brighter one («स्थूलारुन्धतीन्यायेन परशब्दवाच्यपरमात्मानमेव ग्राहयितुं पञ्चकोशकल्पना»). Gopālānanda (a modern commentator) agrees: «यद्यपि यजुरादि वाग्रूपम्, अथापि तत्तद्विषयकज्ञानजनकमनोव्यापार इह यजुरादिशब्देन विवक्षितः».

commentary.q: What do the forms tell us?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: sarvāyuṣa is sarvāyus with the compound-final a: Śaṅkara, «सर्वेषामायुः सर्वायुः, सर्वायुरेव सर्वायुषम्». śārīra is a taddhita of śarīra, ‘in the body’. ṛc and sāman stand in their nominative forms ṛk and sāma.

advaita.text: The selves of breath and mind are, like the body, imagined through ignorance, each the self of the one outside it. Through them the text shows that beings have a self beyond the body, and finally the one Self beyond all five sheaths. The mantras that make up the self of mind are the Self’s consciousness conditioned by mental activity: «मनोवृत्त्युपाधिपरिच्छिन्नं मनोवृत्तिनिष्ठमात्मचैतन्यमनादिनिधनं यजुःशब्दवाच्यम्».

visistadvaita.text: The supreme Self, the cause of space and the rest, is the self of every sheath, which is its body: «अतः तस्माद्वा एतस्मादित्यत्रैव अन्नमयादि आनन्दमयपर्यन्तानां परमात्मा एव आत्मा इत्यवगम्यते». ‘The embodied self of the former’ is that same Self. Rāmānanda: the sheaths are a graded way of pointing to it.

dvaita.text: In the self of mind Saṅkarṣaṇa abides («तस्मिन् सङ्कर्षणः स्थितः»), and the Veda-limbs are his: the head is called Yajus because he takes the sacrifices («शिरस्तस्य यजुर्नाम यज्ञानां हरणात् स्मृतम्»); the trunk, ‘instruction’, is the Pañcarātra («पञ्चरात्रगतं मध्यमादेशाख्यं सुविस्तृतेः»). This comment is printed at the head of Madhva’s note on the next anuvāka in the digital text, after a gap.

schools.disagreement: The decisive difference is the half-line yaḥ pūrvasya: for Śaṅkara the inner sheath is the self of the outer sheath; for Kūranārāyaṇa the supreme Self is the self of every sheath. They also differ on ‘instruction’: the Brāhmaṇa (Śaṅkara), injunction and prohibition (Rāmānanda), the Pañcarātra (Madhva).

parallels.note: Kūranārāyaṇa cites the Śāṇḍilya teaching of the Chāndogya, where the Self is ‘made of mind, with breath for its body’, beside the Taittirīya’s self made of mind.

contemporary.text: The passage makes the shape of the mind out of what the mind recites: the texts it has learned are its head and limbs. Today the mind is shaped by what it reads and scrolls through as surely as by what it once memorised. The passage invites the question of what one’s mind is made of, and whether that is chosen. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Which words, songs or sayings do you know by heart? Do they shape how you think?
reflect.deeper: Is the self of breath ‘the self of the self of food’, or is something else the self of both? What turns on the answer?
reflect.practice: Watch the breath for a minute, then notice the thoughts that ride on it, as the text places mind within breath.

references.text: Madhva’s digital text does not print lines 1–10 of this anuvāka as mūla (corrections.json records this as an omission of the digital witness); his comment on the self of mind stands at the start of his note on 2.4, after a gap marked ‘….’.
Kūranārāyaṇa and Rāmānanda both cite the Kauṣītaki (‘as long as breath dwells in this body, so long is there life’) for ‘breath is the life of beings’; it is reported as cited by them.

flags.note: yaḥ pūrvasya: the self of the outer sheath (Śaṅkara) or the supreme Self that is the self of all the sheaths (Kūranārāyaṇa, Gopālānanda, Rāmānanda). The literal translation keeps the ambiguity.
The padaccheda writes एष before पूर्णः (not the pausal एषः), as in 2.2, because of a limitation of the sandhi checker.

Madhva’s comment on the self of mind is assigned to 2.3 on its content (Saṅkarṣaṇa in the self of mind; the Yajus as head); in the digital text it opens his note on 2.4, and the comment on the self of breath before it is missing.
